claims.source: Despite its lower binding affinity for MOR (Lewanowitsch and Irvine, 2003), NLXM has been shown to reverse opioid-induced hypoventilation and brain hypoxia in rodent models (Lewanowitsch and Irvine, 2002; Perekopskiy et al., 2020; Henderson et al., 2013), suggesting that peripheral opioid receptors may play a greater role in OIRD than previously thought.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewanowitsch and Irvine, 2002; Perekopskiy et al., 2020; Henderson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Intravenous fentanyl at 20 and 50 µg/kg produced rapid decreases in oxygen saturation, heart rate, and respiratory rate.
claims.source: In comparison, both 20 and 50 µg/kg fentanyl produced rapid decreases in oxygen saturation, heart rate, and respiratory rate, with the largest decrease occurring after 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claims.claim: Rats given 50 µg/kg fentanyl exhibited a significantly lower nadir in oxygen saturation compared to 20 µg/kg.
claims.source: Rats given 50 µg/kg fentanyl exhibited a significantly lower nadir in oxygen saturation (Figure 1E) and respiratory rate (Figure 1I) compared to 20 µg/kg.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1I.

claims.claim: The recovery time was significantly longer in rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl compared to 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: In addition, the recovery time was significantly longer in rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl compared to 20 µg/kg fentanyl (Figure 1F, J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1J.

claims.claim: A significant increase in Fos-IR was observed in the nTS after 2 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: A significant increase in Fos-IR was observed after 2 µg/kg fentanyl (Figure 1L), a dose that did not induce cardiorespiratory depression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claims.claim: Further dose-dependent increases in Fos-IR in the nTS were observed after 20 and 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: Further dose-dependent increases in Fos-IR were observed after 20 and 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claims.claim: Catecholaminergic nTS neurons exhibited increased Fos-IR after 2 µg/kg fentanyl and were further activated at the highest dose of fentanyl (50 µg/kg).
claims.source: These cells exhibited increased Fos-IR after 2 µg/kg fentanyl and were further activated at the highest dose of fentanyl (50 µg/kg).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claims.claim: Neither dose of NLXM (1 or 5 mg/kg) was detected within the central nervous system at 2 or 10 min after administration.
claims.source: Neither dose of NLXM was detected within the central nervous system at either time point evaluated (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by biodistribution data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: NLX was not detected in NLXM-treated groups.
claims.source: Importantly, NLX was not detected in these NLXM-treated groups.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by biodistribution data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: Rats that received intravenous NLX exhibited significant, time-dependent detection of NLX in both plasma and brain samples.
claims.source: In comparison, rats that received intravenous NLX exhibited significant, time-dependent detection of NLX in both plasma and brain samples (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by biodistribution data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Neither NLX nor NLXM significantly altered cardiorespiratory parameters from their baseline parameters.
claims.source: Data indicate that neither NLX nor NLXM significantly altered cardiorespiratory parameters from their baseline parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J.

claims.claim: In rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM pretreatment prevented bradycardic and hypoventilatory responses to fentanyl.
claims.source: In rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM pretreatment prevented bradycardic and hypoventilatory responses to fentanyl (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the nadir or duration between NLX (1 mg/kg) and NLXM (1 mg/kg) pretreated rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: For all parameters, saline-pretreated rats exhibited lower nadir values than NLX- and NLXM-pretreated rats, and there was no significant difference in the nadir or duration between NLX (1 mg/kg) and NLXM (1 mg/kg) pretreated rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl (Figure 3E–J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-J.

claims.claim: In rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM pretreatment was unable to prevent the initial decrease in oxygen saturation and heart rate.
claims.source: In rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM pretreatment was unable to prevent the initial decrease in oxygen saturation and heart rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and 1G.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with 5 mg/kg NLXM attenuated cardiorespiratory depression induced by 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: A higher dose of NLXM (5 mg/kg), which does not cross the blood–brain barrier (Figure 2C), was then used in a separate group of animals that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl. Pretreatment with 5 mg/kg NLXM attenuated cardiorespiratory depression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Peripheral MOR antagonism can sufficiently prevent OIRD by 20 µg/kg fentanyl and strongly attenuates OIRD evoked by 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that peripheral MOR antagonism can sufficiently prevent OIRD by 20 µg/kg fentanyl and strongly attenuates OIRD evoked by 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing NLXM's effects on cardiorespiratory parameters.

claims.claim: Blocking peripheral MOR signaling with NLXM did not decrease fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activation.
claims.source: Blocking peripheral MOR signaling with NLXM did not decrease fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activation, while NLX, which blocks both central and peripheral MORs, resulted in a significant reduction in nTS activation (Figure 3L, M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3L and 3M.

claims.claim: NLX, which blocks both central and peripheral MORs, resulted in a significant reduction in nTS activation.
claims.source: Blocking peripheral MOR signaling with NLXM did not decrease fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activation, while NLX, which blocks both central and peripheral MORs, resulted in a significant reduction in nTS activation (Figure 3L, M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3L and 3M.

claims.claim: In rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl, both intravenous NLX (1 mg/kg) and NLXM (1 mg/kg) restored cardiorespiratory values to baseline significantly faster than saline-pretreated animals.
claims.source: In rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl, both intravenous NLX (1 mg/kg) and NLXM (1 mg/kg) restored cardiorespiratory values to baseline significantly faster than saline-pretreated animals (Figure 4F, H, J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, 4H, and 4J.

claims.claim: The reversal of cardiorespiratory parameters by NLXM was similar to NLX in rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: This reversal of cardiorespiratory parameters was similar between NLX- and NLXM-treated animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl, NLX rapidly restored all physiological parameters to their baseline values.
claims.source: In rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl, NLX rapidly restored all physiological parameters to their baseline values (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, H, J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, 1H, and 1J.

claims.claim: A higher dose of 5 mg/kg NLXM fully reversed the fentanyl-induced bradycardia and hypoventilation in rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: While 1 mg/kg NLXM did not sufficiently reverse the OIRD induced by 50 µg/kg fentanyl (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), a higher dose of 5 mg/kg NLXM fully reversed the fentanyl-induced bradycardia and hypoventilation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Blocking peripheral MORs sufficiently reverses OIRD at both moderate and high doses of fentanyl.
claims.source: Thus, blocking peripheral MORs sufficiently reverses OIRD at both moderate and high doses of fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing NLXM's reversal effects.

claims.claim: A similar degree of nTS neuronal activation was observed in all groups regardless of MOR antagonist administered after fentanyl.
claims.source: At both doses of fentanyl administered, a similar degree of nTS neuronal activation was observed in all groups regardless of MOR antagonist administered after fentanyl (Figure 4L, M; Figure 4—figure supplement 1L, M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4L, 4M, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1L, 1M.

claims.claim: Even a brief period of fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression is sufficient to induce robust activation of nTS neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, these data suggest that even a brief period of fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression is sufficient to induce robust activation of nTS neurons, and this subsequent MOR antagonism has no additional effect to increase nTS activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: During the post-conditioning test, NLX-treated animals spent significantly less time in the NLX-paired compartment.
claims.source: During the post-conditioning test, NLX-treated animals spent significantly less time in the NLX-paired compartment, suggesting that the reversal of OIRD on the conditioning day was aversive.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: CPA behavior was not observed in rats that received NLXM at either dose.
claims.source: This CPA behavior was not observed in rats that received NLXM at either dose (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: A single conditioning session with fentanyl administered in the home cage followed by saline in the compartment did not produce a preference or aversion to the saline-paired compartment.
claims.source: Importantly, a single conditioning session with fentanyl administered in the home cage followed by saline in the compartment instead of an MOR antagonist did not produce a preference or aversion to the saline-paired compartment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Neither NLX nor NLXM produced a preference nor aversion to the MOR antagonist-paired compartment when given after saline in the home cage.
claims.source: Neither antagonist produced a preference nor aversion to the MOR antagonist-paired compartment (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Fentanyl (20 µg/kg) infusion induced a biphasic activity profile in nTS neurons, characterized by an initial robust increase (Early Response) followed by a decrease below baseline (Late Response).
claims.source: Fentanyl (20 µg/kg) infusion induced a biphasic activity profile in nTS neurons, characterized by an initial robust increase (Early Response) followed by a decrease below baseline (Late Response, Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with NLXM (5 mg/kg) attenuated both phases of the fentanyl-induced changes in neuronal activity.
claims.source: Pretreatment with NLXM (5 mg/kg) attenuated both phases of the fentanyl-induced changes in neuronal activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: No significant fentanyl-induced change in AUC was observed in NLXM-pretreated rats at either time point.
claims.source: In contrast, no significant fentanyl-induced change in AUC was observed in NLXM-pretreated rats at either time point, indicating that changes in fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activity are strongly mediated by peripheral MORs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Changes in fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activity are strongly mediated by peripheral MORs.
claims.source: In contrast, no significant fentanyl-induced change in AUC was observed in NLXM-pretreated rats at either time point, indicating that changes in fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activity are strongly mediated by peripheral MORs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fiber photometry data showing NLXM's effects.

claims.claim: Both NLX and NLXM enhanced nTS activity above baseline during the late recovery period.
claims.source: However, both NLX and NLXM enhanced nTS activity above baseline during the late recovery period (Figure 6F, G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 6F and 6G.

claims.claim: Peripheral MOR antagonism is sufficient to reverse the fentanyl-induced decrease in nTS neuronal activity.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that peripheral MOR antagonism is sufficient to reverse the fentanyl-induced decrease in nTS neuronal activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fiber photometry data.

claims.claim: Fentanyl induces OIRD via disruption of visceral afferent signaling to the nTS.
claims.source: Nevertheless, our data support a mechanism by which fentanyl induces OIRD via disruption of visceral afferent signaling to the nTS, thereby leading to prolonged OIRD due to suppression of physiological reflex responses that would be normally engaged in response to systemic hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental findings including photometry and cardiorespiratory data.

claims.claim: The nTS plays an essential role in the regulation of basal- and reflex-evoked cardiorespiratory function.
claims.source: The nTS plays an essential role in the regulation of basal- and reflex-evoked cardiorespiratory function (Andresen and Kunze, 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Andresen and Kunze, 1994.

claims.claim: Activation of MOR in the nTS has been shown to blunt hypoxic ventilatory responses following MOR agonism in the nTS.
claims.source: Activation of MOR in the nTS has been shown to blunt hypoxic ventilatory responses following MOR agonism in the nTS (Zhuang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhuang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The degree of fentanyl-induced Fos-IR in the nTS resembles what is observed after acute exposure to hypoxic air.
claims.source: The degree of fentanyl-induced Fos-IR in the nTS resembles what is observed after acute exposure to hypoxic air (Montandon et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 1981).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montandon et al., 2011 and Cohen et al., 1981.

claims.claim: Glutamate is the primary neurotransmitter released from sensory afferent fibers into the nTS.
claims.source: Glutamate is the primary neurotransmitter released from sensory afferent fibers into the nTS (Andresen and Kunze, 1994; Talman et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andresen and Kunze, 1994 and Talman et al., 1980.

claims.claim: Intra-nTS application of opioid agonists have been shown to reduce glutamate release and calcium channels via presynaptic mechanisms.
claims.source: While intra-nTS application of opioid agonists have been shown to reduce glutamate release and calcium channels via presynaptic mechanisms (Cui et al., 2012; Rhim and Miller, 1994), opioids also have been shown to induce a similar biphasic action of Ca2+-dependent spikes in the nodose ganglion (Higashi et al., 1982) that resembles what we observed in GCaMP-expressing nTS cells after intravenous fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2012 and Rhim and Miller, 1994.

claims.claim: Opioids have been shown to induce a similar biphasic action of Ca2+-dependent spikes in the nodose ganglion.
claims.source: While intra-nTS application of opioid agonists have been shown to reduce glutamate release and calcium channels via presynaptic mechanisms (Cui et al., 2012; Rhim and Miller, 1994), opioids also have been shown to induce a similar biphasic action of Ca2+-dependent spikes in the nodose ganglion (Higashi et al., 1982) that resembles what we observed in GCaMP-expressing nTS cells after intravenous fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Higashi et al., 1982.

claims.claim: NLXM strongly attenuated the fentanyl-induced excitatory wave observed in GCaMP-expressing nTS neurons, suggesting that MOR-expressing peripheral afferents mediate this transient activation of nTS neurons.
claims.source: NLXM strongly attenuated the fentanyl-induced excitatory wave observed in GCaMP-expressing nTS neurons, suggesting that MOR-expressing peripheral afferents mediate this transient activation of nTS neurons, even if the primary effect of fentanyl is to inhibit the nTS and suppress cardiorespiratory reflex function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fiber photometry data.

claims.claim: The nTS contains a large population of second-order GABAergic interneurons that receive direct inputs from visceral afferents.
claims.source: The nTS contains a large population of second-order GABAergic interneurons that receive direct inputs from visceral afferents (Bailey et al., 2008), and hypoxia activates these cells (King et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2008 and King et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Hypoxia activates GABAergic interneurons in the nTS.
claims.source: The nTS contains a large population of second-order GABAergic interneurons that receive direct inputs from visceral afferents (Bailey et al., 2008), and hypoxia activates these cells (King et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to King et al., 2012.

claims.claim: nTS MOR agonists suppress the activity of GABAergic interneurons, primarily via presynaptic mechanisms.
claims.source: nTS MOR agonists suppress the activity of these cells, primarily via presynaptic mechanisms (Boxwell et al., 2013), although postsynaptic mechanisms have been reported (Glatzer and Smith, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boxwell et al., 2013 and Glatzer and Smith, 2005.

claims.claim: Visceral afferents activate catecholaminergic nTS neurons.
claims.source: Similarly, visceral afferents also activate catecholaminergic nTS neurons (Appleyard et al., 2007), which are critical for the generation of hypoxia-evoked cardiorespiratory responses (King et al., 2015; Bathina et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Appleyard et al., 2007, King et al., 2015, and Bathina et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Catecholaminergic nTS neurons are critical for the generation of hypoxia-evoked cardiorespiratory responses.
claims.source: Similarly, visceral afferents also activate catecholaminergic nTS neurons (Appleyard et al., 2007), which are critical for the generation of hypoxia-evoked cardiorespiratory responses (King et al., 2015; Bathina et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to King et al., 2015 and Bathina et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Opioids inhibit visceral afferent transmission to catecholaminergic nTS neurons, primarily via a presynaptic mechanism.
claims.source: Opioids inhibit visceral afferent transmission to this cell group, primarily via a presynaptic mechanism (Cui et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Robust Fos expression was observed in catecholaminergic nTS neurons at all doses of fentanyl examined.
claims.source: In the present study, we observed robust Fos expression in these cells at all doses of fentanyl examined.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1M.

claims.claim: nTS dysfunction, via MOR-expressing peripheral inputs that terminate within this region, represents the first central site of fentanyl-induced dysfunction.
claims.source: These findings raise the possibility that nTS dysfunction, via MOR-expressing peripheral inputs that terminate within this region, represents the first central site of fentanyl-induced dysfunction, ultimately leading to downstream effects in other brain regions that contribute to diminished autonomic and cardiorespiratory responses that contribute to the duration of OIRD.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation derived from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Peripheral opioid receptor antagonists are already prescribed for patients undergoing chemotherapy to alleviate side effects such as opioid-induced constipation.
claims.source: Notably, peripheral opioid receptor antagonists are already prescribed for patients undergoing chemotherapy to alleviate side effects such as opioid-induced constipation (Floettmann et al., 2017; Pergolizzi et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Floettmann et al., 2017 and Pergolizzi et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Peripheral MOR antagonists like NLXM could potentially be utilized in treatment strategies for managing patients with OUD.
claims.source: Importantly, our data demonstrate that peripheral MOR antagonism appears to reverse OIRD without triggering unwanted effects of withdrawal that occur following NLX administration, suggesting that peripheral MOR antagonists like NLXM could potentially be utilized in treatment strategies for managing patients with OUD.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation derived from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Baseline cardiorespiratory parameters were similar between male and female rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: As shown in Supplementary file 1A, baseline cardiorespiratory parameters were similar between male and female rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1A.

claims.claim: There was a small but significant difference in basal heart rate in female rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: There was a small but significant difference in basal heart rate in female rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl (Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1B.

claims.claim: No sex differences were observed in the nadir or recovery time in rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: Overall, we observed no sex differences in the nadir or recovery time in rats that received 20 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1C, D.

claims.claim: Female rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl exhibited a significantly longer recovery of respiratory rate.
claims.source: Female rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl exhibited a significantly longer recovery of respiratory rate, although oxygen saturation and heart rate recover times were similar to males (Supplementary file 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1C, D.

claims.claim: Catecholaminergic nTS neurons are critical for full expression of hypoxia-evoked cardiorespiratory responses.
claims.source: We evaluated a subpopulation of catecholaminergic nTS neurons, which are critical for full expression of hypoxia-evoked cardiorespiratory responses (King et al., 2012; King et al., 2015) for activation after intravenous fentanyl (Figure 1M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to King et al., 2012 and King et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Neither saline nor 2 µg/kg fentanyl evoked a significant change in cardiorespiratory parameters.
claims.source: Neither saline nor 2 µg/kg fentanyl evoked a significant change in cardiorespiratory parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The nadir of bradycardia was similar between 20 and 50 µg/kg fentanyl-treated rats.
claims.source: The nadir of bradycardia was similar between 20 and 50 µg/kg rats (Figure 1G), although the duration of the response was significantly longer in rats that received the highest dose of fentanyl (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claims.claim: The duration of bradycardia was significantly longer in rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl compared to 20 µg/kg.
claims.source: The nadir of bradycardia was similar between 20 and 50 µg/kg rats (Figure 1G), although the duration of the response was significantly longer in rats that received the highest dose of fentanyl (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: NLX pretreatment completely blocked the decrease in cardiorespiratory parameters at both 20 and 50 µg/kg doses of fentanyl.
claims.source: As expected, NLX pretreatment completely blocked the decrease in cardiorespiratory parameters at both 20 and 50 µg/kg doses of fentanyl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The time to restore cardiorespiratory parameters to baseline after 5 mg/kg NLXM was not significantly different than NLX in rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: The time to restore parameters to baseline was not significantly different than NLX.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Saline pretreatment evoked the highest degree of fentanyl-induced Fos-IR in the nTS, including in a subpopulation of TH-IR neurons.
claims.source: Saline pretreatment evoked the highest degree of fentanyl-induced Fos-IR in the nTS, including in a subpopulation of TH-IR neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3K-M.

claims.claim: Around 30% of TH-IR neurons displayed Fos-IR in NLX-pretreated rats that received 50 µg/kg fentanyl.
claims.source: This degree of activation was also observed in catecholaminergic cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M), although around 30% of TH-IR neurons also displayed Fos-IR in NLX-pretreated rats.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1M.

claims.claim: The fentanyl-induced nadir in all physiological parameters prior to intravenous administration of saline, NLX, or NLXM was similar between groups.
claims.source: The fentanyl-induced nadir in all physiological parameters prior to intravenous administration of saline, NLX, or NLXM was similar between groups.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E, 4G, 4I.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in the number of Fos-IR cells or the percentage of TH-IR cells expressing Fos-IR between groups that received fentanyl followed by saline, NLX, or NLXM.
claims.source: There were no significant differences in the number of Fos-IR cells or the percentage of TH-IR cells expressing Fos-IR between groups.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4L and 4M.

claims.claim: NLX-mediated reversal of OIRD caused a CPA, as shown by a significant decrease in time spent in the NLX-associated compartment.
claims.source: In this study, we demonstrate that NLX-mediated reversal of OIRD caused a CPA, as shown by a significant decrease in time spent in the NLX-associated compartment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The aversive response to NLX is likely the result of the induction of withdrawal symptoms that occur following antagonism of MOR in central reward pathways.
claims.source: This is likely the result of the induction of withdrawal symptoms that occur following antagonism of MOR in central reward pathways (Lewanowitsch and Irvine, 2002; Lai et al., 2021; Katovich et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference supported by citations to Lewanowitsch and Irvine, 2002; Lai et al., 2021; Katovich et al., 1986.

claims.claim: Alleviating fentanyl-induced respiratory distress without antagonizing central MOR may mitigate the aversive state produced by NLX.
claims.source: These data suggest that alleviating fentanyl-induced respiratory distress without antagonizing central MOR may mitigate the aversive state produced by NLX.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the CPA data.

claims.claim: Sex differences due to fentanyl are relatively minimal compared to other opioids such as heroin.
claims.source: Overall, we observed relatively minimal sex differences in basal and fentanyl-induced changes in cardiorespiratory depression, which is consistent with a previous report showing that sex differences due to fentanyl are relatively minimal compared to other opioids such as heroin (Marchette et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marchette et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Previous reports have shown sexually dimorphic differences in fentanyl-induced conditioned place preference, with higher doses of fentanyl affecting females only.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown sexually dimorphic differences in fentanyl-induced conditioned place preference, with higher doses of fentanyl affecting females only (Knauss et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knauss et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Fentanyl administered to male and female rats in the home cage followed by saline in the CPA box produced neither a preference nor aversion in either sex.
claims.source: In present study, we administered fentanyl to male and female rats in the home cage followed by saline in the CPA box and observed neither a preference nor aversion in either sex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The results obtained during OIRD-mediated reversal via NLX or NLXM are driven by effects within the CPA box and are not influenced by the rewarding properties of fentanyl itself.
claims.source: This suggests that the results obtained during OIRD-mediated reversal via NLX or NLXM are driven by effects within the CPA box and are not influenced by the rewarding properties of fentanyl itself.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the CPA data.

claims.claim: Previous reports have shown that NLX can be detected centrally after a subcutaneous injection of NLXM.
claims.source: While previous reports have shown that NLX can be detected centrally after a subcutaneous injection of NLXM (Perekopskiy et al., 2020), we observed no detectable amount of NLX or NLXM in brain tissue of rats that received intravenous NLXM at either dose or time point.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perekopskiy et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The proximity of the nTS to the circumventricular organ area postrema raises the possibility that fentanyl can access the central nervous system via the area postrema to influence neuronal activation.
claims.source: Given the proximity of the nTS to the circumventricular organ area postrema (Price et al., 2008), this raises the possibility that fentanyl can access the central nervous system via the area postrema to influence neuronal activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to Price et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The lack of a CPA following NLXM-mediated reversal of OIRD supports the biodistribution data showing no NLXM detection in brain samples.
claims.source: However, our data showing the lack of a CPA following NLXM-mediated reversal of OIRD support our biodistribution data showing no NLXM detection in brain samples that the observed effects primarily involve fentanyl actions at MOR located in peripheral sites.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the CPA and biodistribution data.

claims.claim: Peripheral MOR antagonism with NLXM has been shown to partially reverse opioid-induced analgesia.
claims.source: Similar to NLX, peripheral MOR antagonism with NLXM has been shown to partially reverse opioid-induced analgesia (Lewanowitsch and Irvine, 2002; Spahn et al., 2017) which may pose limitations for pain management.

results.result: Intravenous fentanyl induces dose-dependent cardiorespiratory depression and nTS neuronal activation. Fentanyl at 20 and 50 µg/kg produced rapid decreases in oxygen saturation, heart rate, and respiratory rate, with 50 µg/kg causing significantly lower nadirs and longer recovery times. Fos-IR in the nTS increased dose-dependently, including in catecholaminergic neurons, even at 2 µg/kg which did not induce cardiorespiratory depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32, C84-C86 are supported by experimental data from Figure 1 showing dose-dependent effects on cardiorespiratory parameters and nTS activation. The data include appropriate controls (saline, 2 µg/kg), statistical analyses, and consistent findings across multiple parameters. The observation that nTS activation occurs at sub-threshold doses for respiratory depression is particularly well-documented.

results.result: NLXM does not cross the blood-brain barrier and does not alter baseline cardiorespiratory parameters. Biodistribution studies confirmed that neither 1 nor 5 mg/kg NLXM was detected in the CNS at 2 or 10 minutes post-administration, with no conversion to NLX detected. In contrast, NLX was detected in both plasma and brain. Neither NLX nor NLXM altered baseline cardiorespiratory parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 are well-supported by biodistribution data (Figure 2) and baseline cardiorespiratory measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The pharmacokinetic analysis at two time points provides strong evidence for peripheral restriction of NLXM. The lack of NLX detection in NLXM-treated animals rules out metabolic conversion as a confound.

results.result: Peripheral MOR antagonism with NLXM prevents fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression in a dose-dependent manner. NLXM (1 mg/kg) completely prevented OIRD induced by 20 µg/kg fentanyl, with efficacy comparable to NLX. For 50 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM was partially effective, while 5 mg/kg NLXM provided prevention comparable to NLX.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41, C87 are supported by comprehensive cardiorespiratory data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures. The dose-response relationship is well-characterized, with appropriate statistical comparisons between NLXM, NLX, and saline controls. The finding that peripheral MOR antagonism can prevent OIRD is a major result, though the mechanism requires higher doses for higher fentanyl doses.

results.result: NLXM pretreatment does not reduce fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activation, while NLX significantly reduces it. Saline and NLXM-pretreated rats showed similar high levels of Fos-IR in the nTS after fentanyl, including in catecholaminergic neurons. NLX pretreatment resulted in significantly lower nTS activation, though approximately 30% of TH-IR neurons still showed Fos-IR at the highest fentanyl dose.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43, C89-C90 are supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3K-M and supplementary figures. The differential effects of NLXM vs. NLX on nTS activation provide important mechanistic insight, suggesting that peripheral MOR blockade prevents cardiorespiratory depression without preventing central nTS activation, likely due to hypoxia-induced activation.

results.result: Peripheral MOR antagonism with NLXM reverses established fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression comparably to NLX. Both NLXM (1 mg/kg) and NLX (1 mg/kg) restored cardiorespiratory parameters to baseline significantly faster than saline after 20 µg/kg fentanyl. For 50 µg/kg fentanyl, 5 mg/kg NLXM fully reversed OIRD with recovery times comparable to NLX.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48, C88, C91, C113 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and supplementary figures. The reversal experiments demonstrate therapeutic efficacy of peripheral MOR antagonism, with appropriate dose-response relationships. The similar nadirs before antagonist administration (C91) confirm that groups were comparable at baseline, strengthening the conclusions about reversal efficacy.

results.result: Brief fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression is sufficient to induce robust nTS activation regardless of subsequent MOR antagonist treatment. Similar degrees of Fos-IR were observed in all groups (saline, NLX, NLXM) when antagonists were administered after fentanyl, suggesting that even brief OIRD triggers nTS activation that is not further modulated by antagonist treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50, C92 are supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4L-M and supplementary figures. This finding contrasts with the pretreatment experiments and suggests that nTS activation is driven by the hypoxic episode itself rather than ongoing MOR signaling. The interpretation is logical and well-supported by the data.

results.result: NLXM-mediated reversal of OIRD does not produce conditioned place aversion, unlike NLX. NLX-treated animals showed significant CPA (decreased time in NLX-paired compartment), while NLXM at both doses did not produce aversion. Fentanyl alone or antagonists alone (without fentanyl) did not produce preference or aversion, confirming that the NLX aversion is specific to OIRD reversal.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54, C93, C98-C99 are well-supported by CPA data in Figure 5. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (fentanyl alone, antagonists alone) that rule out alternative explanations. The lack of aversion with NLXM is a critical finding for therapeutic potential, suggesting peripheral MOR antagonism avoids CNS-mediated withdrawal symptoms.

results.result: Fentanyl induces a biphasic activity profile in nTS neurons that is mediated by peripheral MORs. Fiber photometry revealed an initial robust increase (Early Response) followed by prolonged decrease below baseline (Late Response) after 20 µg/kg fentanyl. NLXM (5 mg/kg) pretreatment attenuated both phases, with no significant changes in AUC at either time point, indicating peripheral MOR mediation of these responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C109-C110 are supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 6D-E. The biphasic response is clearly demonstrated with appropriate temporal resolution. The attenuation by NLXM provides strong evidence for peripheral MOR involvement. However, the experiments were conducted under isoflurane anesthesia, which is acknowledged as a limitation that could influence the observed responses.

results.result: Both NLX and NLXM reverse fentanyl-induced suppression of nTS neuronal activity, with NLXM showing slower but eventually complete restoration. During late recovery, both antagonists enhanced nTS activity above baseline. NLXM-mediated reversal was slower than NLX during early recovery but achieved similar enhancement during late recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60, C112 are supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 6F-G. The temporal dynamics of recovery provide mechanistic insight into how peripheral vs. central MOR antagonism affects nTS function. The slower recovery with NLXM is consistent with its peripheral restriction and lower binding affinity, yet the eventual restoration supports its therapeutic potential.

results.result: Peripheral MOR antagonism with NLXM represents a promising therapeutic strategy for OIRD that avoids CNS-mediated aversion. NLXM both prevented and reversed OIRD comparably to NLX, indicating substantial peripheral MOR involvement. Unlike NLX, NLXM did not produce aversive behaviors, suggesting it could manage OIRD while sparing withdrawal symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C8-C9 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence from cardiorespiratory, behavioral, and neurophysiological experiments. The therapeutic implications (C9) are appropriately framed as potential rather than proven, acknowledging that clinical translation requires further investigation.

results.result: The nTS represents a critical site of peripheral MOR-mediated dysfunction during OIRD. Fentanyl-induced biphasic nTS activity is attenuated by NLXM, suggesting peripheral afferent involvement. The prolonged suppression of nTS activity may contribute to OIRD duration by disrupting visceral afferent signaling and suppressing hypoxia-responsive reflexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C61, C68, C76, C111, C114 involve mechanistic interpretations that are partially supported but contain speculative elements. While the photometry data clearly show NLXM effects on nTS activity, the causal relationship between nTS suppression and OIRD duration is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The proposal that nTS dysfunction is the 'first central site' (C76) is speculative and would require additional experiments (e.g., selective nTS manipulations) to confirm.

results.result: Sex differences in fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory responses are minimal. Baseline parameters were similar between males and females for 20 µg/kg fentanyl, with a small difference in basal heart rate at 50 µg/kg. No sex differences were observed in nadir or recovery time at 20 µg/kg, though females showed longer respiratory rate recovery at 50 µg/kg.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82, C96 are supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and are consistent with prior literature (Marchette et al., 2023). The analysis appropriately includes both sexes and reports the limited differences observed. However, the photometry experiments could not fully evaluate sex differences due to high attrition rates, which is acknowledged as a limitation.

results.result: The aversive response to NLX likely results from withdrawal symptoms due to central MOR antagonism, while NLXM avoids this by remaining peripherally restricted. The lack of CPA with NLXM supports the biodistribution data showing no CNS penetration and suggests effects are mediated by peripheral MORs.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95, C102 represent reasonable mechanistic interpretations supported by the CPA and biodistribution data, along with citations to prior literature on NLX-induced withdrawal. The inference that peripheral restriction explains the lack of aversion is logical and consistent with the pharmacological properties of NLXM.

results.result: Isoflurane anesthesia may influence nTS responses and could contribute to observed effects in photometry experiments. Isoflurane suppresses glutamatergic transmission, enhances GABAergic transmission, and induces cFos expression in the nTS. Sex differences in anesthetic responses have also been reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by appropriate citations and represent important methodological considerations. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation, noting that chronic fiber implantation in the nTS is not feasible in conscious animals. This caveat is important for interpreting the photometry results.

results.result: The mechanisms underlying fentanyl-induced Fos-IR in the nTS remain unclear and may involve multiple pathways. Possible mechanisms include enhanced chemoreceptor afferent signaling, direct MOR signaling within the nTS, or opioid-induced disinhibition of nTS circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 are explicitly speculative and acknowledge uncertainty about mechanisms. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, these claims represent hypotheses for future investigation rather than supported conclusions. The authors appropriately frame these as possibilities rather than established mechanisms.

results.result: Background claims about the opioid epidemic, fentanyl pharmacology, OIRD mechanisms, and NLXM properties. These include the scope of OUD, fentanyl's role in overdose deaths, its pharmacokinetic properties, MOR distribution in respiratory centers and periphery, nTS function, and prior evidence for NLXM's peripheral restriction and efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C26 are background/contextual claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide the scientific foundation for the study but do not represent novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with current understanding of opioid pharmacology and OIRD.

results.result: Literature-based claims about nTS anatomy, physiology, and MOR signaling mechanisms. These include the nTS role in cardiorespiratory regulation, MOR localization on vagal afferents, effects of MOR agonists on nTS neurotransmission, catecholaminergic neuron function, and prior findings with NLXM and NLX.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C75, C83, C100, C103-C108 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide mechanistic context for interpreting the current findings. The authors appropriately integrate prior knowledge with their novel observations. Claim C75 is additionally supported by the current study's data (Figure 1M).

results.result: Peripheral MOR antagonists are already used clinically for opioid-induced constipation, and NLXM could potentially be utilized for managing OUD patients. This represents a translational perspective based on the current findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 combine established clinical practice (C77, supported by citations) with speculative therapeutic potential (C78). While C77 is well-supported, C78 is appropriately framed as potential rather than proven. Clinical translation would require extensive additional studies including safety, efficacy in humans, and comparison with current standard of care.

results.result: The proximity of the nTS to the area postrema raises the possibility that fentanyl could access the CNS via this circumventricular organ to influence neuronal activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 is speculative and not directly tested. While anatomically plausible, the biodistribution data and CPA results argue against significant CNS penetration of NLXM. The authors appropriately present this as a possibility rather than a conclusion, but it remains unresolved and would require additional experiments to address.

results.result: Fentanyl induces dose-dependent cardiorespiratory depression and nTS neuronal activation. At 20 and 50 µg/kg, fentanyl produced rapid decreases in oxygen saturation, heart rate, and respiratory rate, with 50 µg/kg causing significantly lower nadirs and longer recovery times. Even at 2 µg/kg (a dose not inducing cardiorespiratory depression), fentanyl increased Fos-IR in the nTS, with further dose-dependent increases at higher doses, including activation of catecholaminergic nTS neurons.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm the physiological data showing fentanyl-induced respiratory depression. One reviewer states the paper 'reports compelling physiology data supporting the induction of respiratory distress in fentanyl-treated animals.' Another notes 'the experimental design and data interpretation are rigorous and appropriate controls were used.' No concerns were raised about these dose-response findings.

results.result: NLXM does not cross the blood-brain barrier while NLX does. Biodistribution studies showed that neither 1 nor 5 mg/kg NLXM was detected in the CNS at 2 or 10 minutes post-administration, and no conversion to NLX occurred. In contrast, NLX was detected in both plasma and brain samples in a time-dependent manner. Neither antagonist altered baseline cardiorespiratory parameters in drug-naive animals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. One states the work is 'further supported by pharmacokinetic data suggesting that naloxone methiodide does not penetrate into the brain, nor is it metabolized into brain-penetrant naloxone.' Another notes 'the authors demonstrate the peripheral restriction of naloxone methiodide.' No concerns were raised about the biodistribution data.

results.result: NLXM pretreatment prevents fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression comparably to NLX. At 20 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM prevented bradycardic and hypoventilatory responses with no significant difference from NLX pretreatment. At 50 µg/kg fentanyl, 1 mg/kg NLXM was insufficient, but 5 mg/kg NLXM attenuated cardiorespiratory depression, demonstrating that peripheral MOR antagonism can prevent OIRD.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this as a central finding. One states 'both compounds prevented and reversed fentanyl-induced respiratory depression to a comparable degree.' Another notes 'evidence suggesting that naloxone methiodide reverses this respiratory depression is compelling.' The editor describes this as 'compelling and rigorous physiological...evidence supporting this major claim.'

results.result: NLXM reverses established fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression comparably to NLX. At 20 µg/kg fentanyl, both 1 mg/kg NLX and NLXM restored cardiorespiratory parameters significantly faster than saline, with similar efficacy. At 50 µg/kg fentanyl, while 1 mg/kg NLXM was insufficient, 5 mg/kg NLXM fully reversed bradycardia and hypoventilation, demonstrating that blocking peripheral MORs sufficiently reverses OIRD at both moderate and high fentanyl doses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently support the reversal findings. One states 'both compounds prevented and reversed fentanyl-induced respiratory depression to a comparable degree.' Another notes the authors 'address both prevention and reversal of fentanyl-derived respiratory depression.' The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling and rigorous.'

results.result: NLXM-mediated OIRD reversal does not produce conditioned place aversion (CPA) unlike NLX. NLX-treated animals spent significantly less time in the NLX-paired compartment during post-conditioning tests, indicating aversion likely due to withdrawal symptoms from central MOR antagonism. In contrast, NLXM at either dose did not produce CPA, suggesting that peripheral MOR antagonism mitigates the aversive state produced by NLX.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding as a major advantage. One states 'the advantage of peripheral treatments is that they circumvent the withdrawal-like effects of nalaxone.' Another notes 'the result that a peripheral approach for OIRD rescue may side-step severe negative withdrawal symptoms of traditional NLX rescue' as a strength. The editor emphasizes 'significant therapeutic implications given that medications currently used to reverse opioid overdose...produce severe aversive and withdrawal effects.'

results.result: Fentanyl-induced nTS neuronal activation persists regardless of peripheral or central MOR antagonism timing. NLXM pretreatment did not decrease fentanyl-induced nTS Fos-IR, while NLX pretreatment significantly reduced it. When antagonists were administered after fentanyl, similar degrees of nTS activation were observed across all groups, suggesting that even brief fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression is sufficient to robustly activate nTS neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support the nTS activation data. One states 'the authors demonstrated activation of NTS cells using multiple techniques and the study links peripheral activation of mu opioid receptors to central activation of NTS cells.' Another notes the data are 'compelling' and 'rigorous.' No concerns were raised about the Fos-IR findings.

results.result: Fentanyl induces a biphasic activity profile in nTS neurons that is mediated by peripheral MORs. Fiber photometry revealed an initial robust increase (Early Response) followed by a decrease below baseline (Late Response) after 20 µg/kg fentanyl. NLXM pretreatment attenuated both phases, with no significant fentanyl-induced change in AUC, indicating peripheral MOR mediation. Both NLX and NLXM enhanced nTS activity above baseline during late recovery, demonstrating that peripheral MOR antagonism reverses fentanyl-induced nTS inhibition.
results.evaluation: While reviewers affirm the photometry data as compelling, one explicitly states 'the paper would be further strengthened by establishing the functional significance of the altered neural activity detected in the nTS (as measured by cFos and GcAMP/photometry) in the context of opioid-induced respiratory depression.' This indicates the mechanistic interpretation linking nTS activity changes to OIRD requires additional validation.

results.result: Peripheral MORs play a critical role in OIRD, including via ascending inputs to the nTS. The authors propose that fentanyl induces OIRD via disruption of visceral afferent signaling to the nTS, with peripheral MOR antagonism sufficient to prevent and reverse OIRD by overriding central effects. This suggests nTS dysfunction via peripheral MOR-expressing inputs may represent the first central site of fentanyl-induced dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the mechanistic contribution but express reservations. One states 'the paper would be further strengthened by establishing the functional significance of the altered neural activity detected in the nTS.' The editor notes the work 'furthers mechanistic understanding of how peripheral opioid receptors contribute to respiratory depression,' but the lack of direct functional validation (e.g., nTS manipulation experiments) leaves the mechanistic claims incompletely supported.

results.result: Selective peripheral MOR antagonism could be a promising therapeutic strategy for managing OIRD by avoiding CNS-driven withdrawal and aversion. The authors speculate that peripheral MOR antagonists like NLXM could be utilized in treatment strategies for OUD patients, given that peripheral opioid receptor antagonists are already prescribed for opioid-induced constipation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the therapeutic implications. The editor states the findings 'have significant therapeutic implications given that medications currently used to reverse opioid overdose...produce severe aversive and withdrawal effects.' One reviewer calls this 'a massive boon to the OUD community' and notes 'this important study reframes our understanding of successful overdose rescue with a potential for reduced aversive withdrawal effects.' Another acknowledges the work is 'somewhat incremental' since naloxone is already used, but does not dispute the therapeutic potential.

results.result: Sex differences in fentanyl-induced cardiorespiratory depression are minimal. Baseline parameters were similar between males and females at 20 µg/kg fentanyl, with only a small difference in basal heart rate at 50 µg/kg. No sex differences were observed in nadir or recovery time at 20 µg/kg, though females exhibited longer respiratory rate recovery at 50 µg/kg. This is consistent with prior reports showing minimal sex differences for fentanyl compared to other opioids.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the inclusion of both sexes as a strength. One states 'both males and females were used in the experiments' as a positive feature. No concerns were raised about the sex difference analyses or interpretations.

results.result: Background and literature context on opioid use disorders, fentanyl pharmacology, OIRD mechanisms, nTS function, MOR distribution, and prior NLXM studies. These claims establish the scientific rationale and prior knowledge supporting the study's design and interpretation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the background literature or context. The editor notes the work 'reshapes our understanding of opioid-related effects on respiration,' implicitly affirming the contextual framing. No concerns were raised about the cited literature or background claims.

results.result: Interpretive and speculative claims about mechanisms underlying nTS activation, CPA results, and potential routes of fentanyl CNS access. These include speculation about glutamatergic transmission, opioid-induced disinhibition, area postrema involvement, and the contribution of nTS suppression to OIRD duration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly address these speculative mechanistic interpretations. However, one reviewer's request to 'establish the functional significance of the altered neural activity' suggests that mechanistic speculation without direct functional validation is viewed as incomplete. These claims remain uncertain pending additional experimental support.
